findings.headline: Local Government and Housing Ombudsman complaints nearly doubled; indicator of service quality collapse
findings.detail: Upheld Local Government Ombudsman complaints jumped from 27 to 52 (93% increase); Housing Ombudsman maladministration cases rose from 28 to 42 (50% increase). These complaints correlate with the RSH-identified housing failures and indicate systemic deterioration in service quality and governance across the housing function.
findings.matters: Ombudsman complaints are leading indicators of service failure and governance breakdown; rapid escalation suggests systemic issues that may trigger further regulatory action
findings.figures: LGO upheld complaints: 52 (2024-25) vs 27 (2023-24); Housing Ombudsman maladministration: 42 (2024-25) vs 28 (2023-24)
findings.quote: Local Government Ombudsman findings: 52 upheld complaints (2023-24: 27); Housing Ombudsman findings: 42 cases of maladministration or severe maladministration (2023-24: 28)

findings.headline: General fund reserves fell £11m in one year; financial sustainability now depends on unproven transformation savings
findings.detail: The Council's general fund balance fell by £11m during 2024-25 (after a £32m increase in 2023-24). The auditors note the Council 'will need to ensure it achieves savings plans...to minimise the likelihood of a significant pressure on reserves,' particularly in light of anticipated central government funding reductions following funding reform.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion is accelerating; financial sustainability now depends on successful execution of transformation programmes that have not yet been proven to deliver savings
findings.figures: General fund balance fell £11m in 2024-25 (prior year increased £32m); medium-term financial strategy shows no unidentified savings for 2024-27 (down from £11m prior year)
findings.quote: Owing to the financial pressures set out earlier, and planned uses of reserves for investments in services, the Council's overall general fund balance fell by £11m during 2024-25 (£32m increase during 2023-24).

findings.headline: HRA now borrowing to fund capital maintenance rather than self-funding; compounds financial stress
findings.detail: Historically, councils are expected to generate HRA surpluses to self-fund capital investment in homes. However, Southwark is now forced to borrow from PWLB to fund capital investment due to reserve pressures. This creates additional interest charges, further compounding the HRA's financial sustainability challenge in a self-defeating cycle.
findings.matters: Borrowing to pay for maintenance (rather than new assets) is not sustainable; it signals the council is consuming capital to cover interest, a sign of structural financial imbalance
findings.figures: Quantum of HRA capital borrowing not disclosed; PWLB interest rates are currently elevated
findings.quote: As Councils are expected to generate surpluses to fund capital investment, such as in improving the quality of homes, the pressure in HRA balances means that the Council has now started to borrow to fund capital investment. This generates further interest charges and compounds the financial sustainability issues in the HRA.

findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing issued C3 non-compliant rating; auditor identified significant governance weakness in housing
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing (RSH) issued Southwark a C3 rating (non-compliant; C1 is best, C4 is worst) in November 2024. The auditor has identified a significant weakness in governance arrangements because the Council lacks an up-to-date stock condition survey of its housing (last conducted in 2010), preventing management from understanding the true scale of maintenance obligations. Approximately 30% of homes do not meet the Decent Homes Standard.
findings.matters: C3 rating from the housing regulator signals service failure; lenders must assess likelihood of further enforcement action, potential financial penalties, and costs of remediation works
findings.figures: ~30% of homes do not meet Decent Homes Standard; stock condition survey last conducted in 2010; early survey findings identified 79 severe failures and 22 moderate failures
findings.quote: Southwark Council does not have up to date stock condition information for most of its homes. Southwark Council's last stock condition survey was undertaken in 2010 on a representative sample of 10% general needs, and 20% street properties.

findings.headline: General fund overspent by £18m due to temporary accommodation demand; contingency use jumped to £5.3m
findings.detail: The Council budgeted £355m for the general fund but outturn was £373m—an £18m overspend driven by demand for temporary accommodation due to homelessness. To cover this, the Council deployed £5.3m of contingency reserves (nearly four times the prior year's £1.4m), indicating deteriorating budgetary control and intensifying demand pressures.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation costs are demand-driven and difficult to control; rising contingency use reveals budget accuracy declining and financial pressures mounting faster than anticipated
findings.figures: General fund budget £355m, outturn £373m (£18m overspend); contingency use £5.3m (prior year £1.4m)
findings.quote: Outturn was £373m, the difference in which was driven primarily through demand on temporary accommodation budgets on account of the number of homeless individuals and families in the borough (and London more broadly).

findings.headline: HRA recovery plan relies on one-off measures; risk of deficits reemerging if recurrent savings fail
findings.detail: The HRA achieved a £3.9m surplus in 2024-25 (versus £2.5m deficit in prior year), but the auditors explicitly warn this included non-recurrent income from a one-off service charge collection. They note 'there is a risk of deficits reemerging in the future' and that the Council 'will need to continue rigorously controlling costs to bring the HRA into a recurrent and sustainable surplus position.'
findings.matters: A recovery plan built on temporary measures is not financially sustainable; lenders need assurance that underlying cost structures have been permanently improved
findings.figures: HRA surplus 2024-25: £3.9m (vs deficit £2.5m prior year); part of surplus was one-off service charge collection
findings.quote: Whilst the surplus is positive, some of the contributory factors are non-recurrent in nature (for instance the income was primarily due to one-off collection of service charges) and therefore there is a risk of deficits reemerging in the future.

findings.headline: HRA reserve of £21m is small for a council of this size; reserve declined to risky level
findings.detail: Southwark's Housing Revenue Account reserve stands at only £21m, which the auditors explicitly describe as 'considered small for a Council of this size.' While it increased £4m in 2024-25, the reserve remains inadequate as a buffer against the multiple financial pressures in the HRA, including inflation, interest costs, and building safety remediation.
findings.matters: A small HRA reserve limits the council's ability to absorb shocks or delays in cost control programmes; this is particularly concerning given the regulatory enforcement risk
findings.figures: HRA reserve £21m at 31 March 2025 (up £4m from 2023-24); prior year deficit was £2.5m
findings.quote: At 31 March 2025, the HRA reserve sits at £21m which is considered small for a Council of this size.

findings.headline: New homes programme cut due to high PWLB interest rates making construction financially unviable
findings.detail: Southwark is one of England's largest social landlords with a long-standing political priority to build new homes. However, the Council has been forced to scale back its housing development programme because rising interest rates on PWLB borrowing make new construction unaffordable. It is now exploring alternative delivery models such as buying completed homes from developers rather than building them itself.
findings.matters: A major capital programme being curtailed signals stress on HRA finances and reduced capacity to deliver on housing policy; it also indicates the Council's sensitivity to interest rate movements
findings.figures: Programme value not quantified; relates to PWLB interest rate exposure on housing debt
findings.quote: the Council has been pairing back its new homes programme as it is not considered financially viable.

findings.paper_title: Report: Internal Audit CAFT and HIT Progress Update
findings.headline: Limited assurance audit findings in Adult Social Care are being tracked and addressed by management
findings.detail: Internal audits of Nursing and Residential Care services and waiting list management for older people and people with disabilities received limited assurance ratings. Management has provided updates on progress with agreed management actions to address these findings. Details are set out in Appendix 1, with management attending the committee to answer questions.
findings.matters: Limited assurance in Adult Social Care, typically a significant council budget area, indicates control weaknesses in a high-risk service. Ensuring these findings are properly remediated is important for governance and financial assurance.
findings.figures: Not detailed in main report
findings.quote: management have provided updates on progress with the agreed management actions (see Appendix 1) and will be attending the committee to answer any questions the Committee may have

findings.paper_title: Report: Internal Audit CAFT and HIT Progress Update
findings.headline: Internal Audit Plan for 2026/27 is running behind its planned delivery profile with no reviews yet at draft report stage
findings.detail: The council's Internal Audit Plan, approved in July 2026, is behind the originally anticipated delivery profile. No audit reviews have progressed to draft report stage as of August 2026. The delays are attributed to limited permanent audit resource capacity. The council is recruiting additional staff and procuring external audit support, but acknowledges a risk that further delays could require the plan to be re-profiled during the year.
findings.matters: An audit plan falling behind schedule means governance and control assurance is lagging. If resource or procurement delays persist, some planned audit coverage may not be completed in 2026/27, leaving control gaps unaddressed for a full year.
findings.figures: No reviews at draft report stage as of August 2026; plan approved July 2026
findings.quote: overall delivery against the annual audit plan is currently behind the profile originally anticipated

findings.headline: Funding stays flat while unavoidable cost pressures continue to mount
findings.detail: The council's total funding income remains flat whilst grants decline. Meanwhile, unavoidable pressures accumulate: inflation adjustments, pay awards, contract inflation, and growing demand for services such as temporary accommodation. Council tax and business rates provide some growth but are insufficient to close the gap.
findings.matters: This structural mismatch—flat or declining funding against rising mandatory costs—is not cyclical and cannot be addressed by one-year efficiencies. It signals sustained pressure on reserves and service capacity.
findings.figures: Total income stays flat; grants fall; inflation and TA demand growth identified as significant gap components
findings.quote: But as funding stays flat, costs continue to rise…

findings.headline: Budget gap has grown to £102m over three years (2027-30) driven by government funding formula changes
findings.detail: The council's published February 2026 gap of £80m has now grown to £102m for April 2027 to March 2030. The gap is expanding year on year (£46m in 2026-27, rising to £102m cumulative by 2028-29). Government changes to the funding formula are a primary driver.
findings.matters: A £102m three-year gap represents structural financial stress requiring major savings or external funding to maintain service delivery. This scale of imbalance constrains operational flexibility and creates risk around meeting statutory obligations.
findings.quote: The budget gap for the three years from April 2027 to March 2030 is now estimated at £102m. This follows the Government's changes to our funding formula

findings.headline: Governance framework for tracking transformation programme savings remains outstanding.
findings.detail: The council's medium-term financial plan depends on transformation savings, but governance arrangements to monitor delivery and track financial benefit realisation have not yet been fully established. The recommendation remains outstanding.
findings.matters: Without governance to track achievement, there is material risk that MTFP savings targets are not delivered, leaving budget gaps unfunded.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The Council should ensure it has developed sufficient and appropriate governance arrangements to monitor the delivery and outcome of these transformation programmes, and track financial savings as part of ongoing monitoring of the medium-term financial plan (MTFP).

findings.headline: Unquantified backlog of cyclical works TMOs were paid to perform but did not complete.
findings.detail: The council identified that some Tenant Management Organisations failed to perform cyclical works they were paid for, creating a repair liability. The council has not set out plans to address this backlog or quantify its cost impact.
findings.matters: This represents an unresolved and unquantified capital liability in the HRA; remediation costs could be material and impact future reserves and borrowing.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The Council has not yet set out its plans or intentions for ensuring any backlog of cyclical works are to be performed where TMOs were paid to perform the works but they did not happen.

findings.headline: Major works delivery control framework remains untested after Devon Mansions and Canada Estate scheme failures.
findings.detail: Following documented delivery problems on Devon Mansions and Canada Estate, the council introduced a new control approach in 2024-25. However, it has not independently assessed whether this new approach is actually working or preventing recurrence of past issues. The audit recommendation for independent review remains outstanding.
findings.matters: Past scheme delivery failures and untested new controls represent capital delivery risk; a lender needs assurance that the council can execute major programmes without cost overruns or control failures.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The Council has developed a new approach to managing major works schemes and has rolled out this approach on a trial scheme over the course of 2024-25. The intention is then to apply this new approach on schemes throughout 2025-26 and beyond. The Council has, however, not assessed if this new approach is working effectively and mitigating the issues that arose on the Devon Mansions and Canada Estate schemes.

findings.headline: Material misstatement in HRA dwelling valuations exposed a transposition error in core accounting process.
findings.detail: A transposition error in valuation spreadsheets caused the wrong year's dwelling valuation to be included in the accounts, resulting in a material overall valuation error. The council has since introduced dual-authorisation and locked spreadsheet columns to prevent recurrence, but this signals a control weakness in a core HRA accounting process.
findings.matters: The HRA is a major balance sheet item; a material valuation error indicates insufficient internal controls over fundamental accounting processes that lenders rely on.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: A misstatement was identified in the dwelling valuation because of a transposition error made in the valuation sheets, meaning the wrong year's figure was pulled through into the valuation journal. As a consequence the overall valuation was materially incorrect.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Management Update on Nursing & Residential Care and OPPD Waiting Lists
findings.headline: Medium-risk audit finding: limited proactive financial resilience monitoring of care providers
findings.detail: The audit identified no systemic process for monitoring whether care providers remain financially stable after procurement. The council notes providers are reluctant to disclose financial distress, and annual credit checks have limited value due to reporting lags.
findings.matters: Failure to monitor provider financial health creates risk of sudden provider collapse, disrupting service delivery and forcing emergency procurement at higher cost; particularly relevant for out-of-borough spot placements
findings.figures: No specific providers flagged as at risk
findings.quote: provider financial resilience is reviewed at procurement stage and there is no systemic process for further reviews

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Management Update on Nursing & Residential Care and OPPD Waiting Lists
findings.headline: Capacity and staffing issues causing delays in older people assessments and service provision
findings.detail: OPPD is experiencing delays in assessment processes due to capacity issues, backlogs, and staff absence. The council is undertaking a wider review of its operating model with proposed organizational changes, acknowledging that current capacity is insufficient.
findings.matters: Service delays indicate resource constraints or inefficiency; proposed organizational restructuring suggests the problem is structural, not temporary, and may require investment to resolve
findings.figures: No quantified delays reported
findings.quote: Delays in referral processes due to capacity issues, backlogs, and staff absence; some cases held in triage or allocation pending further information.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Management Update on Nursing & Residential Care and OPPD Waiting Lists
findings.headline: High-risk control weakness: placement fee decisions lack proper oversight and benchmarking
findings.detail: The audit found that placement coordinators are making decisions on fees and uplifts for spot placements without access to proper information, tools, or benchmarking data. The council is developing a framework to address this, to be implemented by 2027-28.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled fee-setting decisions create cost risk and inefficiency; lack of oversight suggests overpayment for services and poor value for money
findings.figures: Framework implementation delayed to 2027-28
findings.quote: decisions on fees and uplifts for spot placements sits with placement coordinators who do not always have the range of information and tools required.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Management Update on Nursing & Residential Care and OPPD Waiting Lists
findings.headline: High-risk finding: over-reliance on spot purchasing for care due to limited in-borough capacity
findings.detail: The council acknowledges a high number of spot placements (largely out-of-borough), indicating limited contracted in-borough capacity. Management actions focus on cost reduction rather than expanding compliant provision, meaning the dependency on spot purchasing is not expected to decrease.
findings.matters: Spot purchasing is typically more expensive and creates market dependency; limited in-borough capacity suggests the council cannot fully meet demand through contracted services and is vulnerable to price inflation
findings.figures: High number of spot placements; limited in-borough capacity noted
findings.quote: Due to limited in borough capacity negotiated arrangements will need to be developed over time and will focus on overall cost reduction rather than increasing the numbers of RCC compliant providers.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Management Update on Nursing & Residential Care and OPPD Waiting Lists
findings.headline: High-risk audit finding: poor data quality and inconsistent processes in OPPD waiting list management
findings.detail: BDO's audit found internal Occupational Therapy audits were inconsistent and not sufficiently documented, and cases were not being removed from waiting lists when no longer needed. This speaks to control weaknesses in case management and data integrity.
findings.matters: Poor data quality in case management creates risk of duplicate or forgotten cases, waste of resources, and gaps in oversight of vulnerable people; signals broader governance weaknesses
findings.figures: No quantified impact reported
findings.quote: Internal Occupational Therapy audits of waiting list were considered inconsistent and not sufficiently documented. The audit identified cases not removed from waiting lists when a service was no longer needed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Management Update on Nursing & Residential Care and OPPD Waiting Lists
findings.headline: Adult social care budget pressures worsening with no additional funding to meet demand
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that rising care costs have created budgetary pressures while demand grows from an ageing population and increased complexity. No additional resources are available, forcing the service to rely on modernizing its operating model and automation rather than capacity increases.
findings.matters: Growing demand pressure in a major council service with frozen resources suggests potential future service cuts, efficiency losses, or overspending if demand cannot be managed through process improvements alone
findings.figures: Growing demand, ageing population, rising complexity; no numbers quantified
findings.quote: increases in the cost of care have created significant budgetary pressures, meaning that no additional resources are available to meet the growth in demand.

findings.headline: £9m uncorrected misstatement: Council accrued for backdated pension contributions without having informed affected staff or established legal obligation
findings.detail: The Council created a £9m accrual to pay backdated pension contributions to staff erroneously not auto-enrolled into the LGPS. However, no accounting obligation existed at the balance sheet date because the Council had not yet informed the affected staff. The auditors requested correction under ISA 450; the Council did not correct this.
findings.matters: A lender needs accurate reserves and liabilities reporting; this indicates either weak financial reporting controls or the council's judgment that a provision should be made before the legal/informational trigger.
findings.figures: £9m uncorrected misstatement
findings.quote: The Council has created an accrual to pay backdated pension contributions to staff who were erroneously not auto-enrolled into the LGPS. However, the Council did not have an accounting obligation to do so at the balance sheet date as it had not yet informed the affected staff.

findings.headline: Major Works governance: prior audit findings on Devon Mansions and Canada Estate schemes; Council's remedial approach not yet independently validated
findings.detail: The auditors identified 'substantial systematic weaknesses in controls in respect of major works schemes' from a detailed review into two major works that occurred during the year. The Council has developed a new approach to major works management but has 'not assessed if this new approach is working effectively.' The auditors' recommendation for independent scrutiny of the new approach was declined by the Council pending February 2026 internal audit.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that the council can deliver complex capital schemes on budget and to specification; unvalidated remedial controls create delivery risk.
findings.figures: Two major works schemes (Devon Mansions and Canada Estate) showed 'substantial systematic weaknesses'; no major works schemes to assess in 2024/25
findings.quote: After year-end, we became aware of a detailed review into two major works that took place during the year which identified substantial systematic weaknesses in controls in respect of major works schemes, where there is a realistic risk that the Council systematically does not have appropriate governance arrangements in relation to contract management.

findings.headline: £4.5m understatement in investment property valuation; auditors attribute to market valuation error not supported by comparatives
findings.detail: The auditors identified and corrected an understatement of one investment property by £4.5m. The property valuation was 'not in line with available market evidence.' Whilst the auditors believed this was a unique case not representative of the portfolio, it indicates a valuation control gap.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in the realizable value of the council's commercial property portfolio (£303m); undervaluation of individual assets suggests the portfolio may carry valuation risk.
findings.figures: £4.5m understatement corrected; investment property portfolio £303m as at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: We identified an understatement of £4.5m which has been corrected due to an asset where, in our view, the valuation was not in line with available market evidence.

findings.headline: Significant weakness in housing governance: Council cannot determine extent of housing estate condition or quantum of works required
findings.detail: The auditors identified a significant Value for Money weakness linked to the Regulator of Social Housing's damning prior-year judgment. The paper states: 'the Council is unable to ascertain the extent to which its housing estate is fit for purpose, or the quantum of works required to bring its estate into good condition.' This creates risk of future RSH penalties and uncertainty over a material financial obligation.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the extent of committed capital works and maintenance liabilities; unknown quantum of housing estate remediation represents unquantified future liability and execution risk.
findings.figures: Housing asset value £3.6bn (dwellings); RSH judgment was 'damning'; penalty not imposed 'because there was a clear commitment by the Council to putting things right'
findings.quote: the Council is unable to ascertain the extent to which its housing estate is fit for purpose, or the quantum of works required to bring its estate into good condition. Consequently there is a risk that the Council does not have effective measures to manage the quality of its estate, handle expectations of residents, or satisfy the RSH's expectations.

findings.headline: £29m understatement in council dwellings valuation due to control failure in beacon group review
findings.detail: A typographical error in the valuation of one beacon group resulted in a factual £29m understatement affecting approximately 700 dwellings. The auditors identify this as evidence of 'weaknesses in the Council's controls to review the asset valuations' — a recurring issue from prior years. The Council receives valuations close to publication date, leaving insufficient time for rigorous review before recording.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance over the accuracy of asset valuations on which borrowing capacity and covenant compliance depend; recurring control failures indicate systemic risk.
findings.figures: £29m understatement corrected; 700 assets affected; 9 beacon groups exceed 600-property guidance maximum (largest contains 2,244 properties)
findings.quote: Consistent with last year, we identified weaknesses in the Council's controls to review the asset valuations and ensure they were prepared using an appropriate methodology. In particular, in selecting our sample for detailed testing Cluttons identified a typographical error in the valuation of one beacon. When extrapolated across the beacon group, a factual £29m understatement of the value of dwellings was identified.

findings.paper_title: Report: HRA Governance and Financial Monitoring
findings.headline: 24% of capital spending funded by borrowing exposes HRA to rising interest costs
findings.detail: In 2025-26, £47.3m of the £198m HRA capital investment (24%) was funded by borrowing. The paper emphasises the 'continued reliance on borrowing to support the programme' and identifies 'higher interest rates' as a significant financial risk. Managing 'affordability, interest costs and the timing of future capital investment' is flagged as requiring careful planning through the HRA Business Plan.
findings.matters: HRA budgets are cash-limited and must be self-funding. Heavy borrowing at rising rates increases debt service costs, squeezing resources available for repairs and maintenance. Each 1% increase in rates costs approximately £3.3m annually on the remaining £332m programme.
findings.figures: £47.3m of £198m capital funded by borrowing (24%); £332m remaining programme borrowing requirement
findings.quote: Of the £198m spent in 2025-26, £47.3m, or 24%, was funded from borrowing. This highlights the continued reliance on borrowing to support the programme and reinforces the need to manage affordability, interest costs and the timing of future capital investment through the HRA Business Plan.

findings.paper_title: Report: HRA Governance and Financial Monitoring
findings.headline: Construction cost inflation and supply chain disruption are significant ongoing risk to capital programme affordability
findings.detail: Geopolitical instability is creating 'volatility in energy markets and supply chains', affecting cost and availability of steel, cement, and mechanical/electrical components. The paper identifies this as a 'significant financial risk' for both repairs and new build programmes, with particular concern that 'reduced market appetite or competition for complex estate renewal schemes' limits councils' ability to control costs through competition.
findings.matters: The HRA's £1.3bn ten-year capital programme is heavily dependent on borrowing (£332m still required). Rising construction costs either reduce scope or increase borrowing need. Reduced contractor competition on complex schemes removes negotiating leverage. This directly threatens capital affordability and programme delivery.
findings.figures: £1.3bn total HIP 2025-26 to 2034-35; £332m remaining borrowing requirement
findings.quote: Construction cost inflation therefore remains a significant financial risk for both Repairs and Maintenance and New Build, with continued pressure on labour, materials and energy costs affecting tender prices, contractor capacity, scheme affordability and the risk of procurement or delivery delays. These factors have direct capital affordability implications for the HRA, including increased capital costs, higher borrowing requirements where costs exceed original assumptions, programme delays and rephasing, and reduced market appetite or competition for complex estate renewal schemes.

findings.paper_title: Report: HRA Governance and Financial Monitoring
findings.headline: Provision recognised for potential refunds from review of historic tenant charges
findings.detail: A provision has been recognised in 2025-26 accounts for estimated refund costs arising from a review of historic tenant charges. Determined using 'updated methodology', it 'reflects the best estimate of the Council's obligations based on information available' but is indicated as subject to ongoing review and refinement as further information emerges.
findings.matters: A provision for refunds signals past billing errors or overcharges requiring financial settlement. The fact it continues to be refined indicates uncertainty about the final liability, creating contingent exposure. Size matters but is not disclosed in this report.
findings.figures: Provision amount not disclosed
findings.quote: A provision has been recognised to reflect the estimated cost of potential refunds arising from a review of historic tenant charges. The provision has been determined using an updated methodology and reflects the best estimate of the Council's obligations based on information available. The provision will continue to be reviewed and refined as further information becomes available.

findings.paper_title: Report: HRA Governance and Financial Monitoring
findings.headline: Revenue income £10.6m below budget, driven by £8.3m temporary accommodation rent policy change and £2.8m void losses
findings.detail: Total HRA revenue income fell £10.6m short of budget in 2025-26. The largest component (£8.3m) came from temporary accommodation properties switched to formula rent from April 2025 under the 2020 Rent Standard, generating an adverse variance 'after routine stock movements.' Void rental losses added £2.8m, though this improved from a £3.5m month 6 forecast.
findings.matters: Large revenue income shortfalls drive deficits and make the HRA dependent on reserves or borrowing. Temporary accommodation income is now outside council control under policy rent-setting, making forecasting harder. Void losses of £2.8m annually on a ring-fenced budget is material.
findings.figures: £10.6m total income below budget; £8.3m from temporary accommodation rent-setting; £2.8m void losses
findings.quote: Total HRA income was £10.6m below budget, driven primarily by the rent-setting position for HRA properties used for temporary accommodation. These have now been set at formula rent from 1 April 2025, in line with the 2020 Rent Standard, which resulted in an £8.3m adverse variance after routine stock movements. In addition, there were rental income losses from empty properties classed as 'Voids', contributing £2.8m to the end of year position.

findings.paper_title: Report: HRA Governance and Financial Monitoring
findings.headline: 2026-27 balanced budget relies partly on one-off measures, not structural solutions
findings.detail: The 2026-27 HRA budget achieves balance only through one-off, non-recurring measures in addition to the £6m savings. The paper acknowledges 'the balanced 2026-27 position relies in part on one-off measures,' requiring particular monitoring through September and December revenue reports to track whether recurring savings are actually being delivered.
findings.matters: One-off measures mask structural deficit. A budget balanced with temporary support indicates 2027-28 will face even larger pressures unless recurring solutions are found. This is the definition of unsustainable financial position.
findings.figures: 2026-27 balance depends partly on one-off measures
findings.quote: This will be particularly important because the balanced 2026-27 position relies in part on one-off measures.

findings.paper_title: Report: HRA Governance and Financial Monitoring
findings.headline: 2026-27 HRA savings requirement jumped to £6m from £2.8m forecast just six months earlier
findings.detail: The 2026-27 budget includes a savings requirement of £6m, more than double the £2.8m reported in the February 2026 cabinet budget report. The increase reflects 'additional inflationary and service growth pressures' on top of the base recovery plan. Delivery will require 'stronger oversight, clear ownership across services and regular challenge through the Budget Recovery Board.'
findings.matters: A 114% increase in required savings within six months indicates budget pressures are accelerating faster than planned. This tests management capability to deliver much larger savings while potentially implementing cuts elsewhere, and signals higher risk of failure to balance.
findings.figures: £6m 2026-27 savings requirement vs £2.8m in February 2026
findings.quote: The 2026-27 HRA budget includes a savings requirement of £6m, an increase from the £2.8m reported in the February 2026 cabinet budget Report. The increase reflects additional inflationary and service growth pressures that need to be managed within the ring-fenced HRA budget.

findings.paper_title: Report: HRA Governance and Financial Monitoring
findings.headline: HRA closed 2025-26 in deficit and remains not yet on a sustainable footing
findings.detail: The HRA ended 2025-26 with a net adverse variance of £1.4m despite improvement from the £7.3m adverse variance at month 6. The paper explicitly confirms that 'the HRA remains under financial pressure and is not yet on a sustainable footing' despite tighter expenditure control. This indicates the recovery plan has not yet returned the account to stability.
findings.matters: A ring-fenced HRA running at deficit must draw reserves or borrow to survive. After years of recovery work, the account remains in deficit, indicating structural pressures are not yet solved and reserve depletion is ongoing.
findings.figures: £1.4m net adverse variance 2025-26; £7.3m adverse variance at month 6
findings.quote: However, the final position confirms that the HRA remains under financial pressure and is not yet on a sustainable footing.

findings.headline: Three-year budget gap of approximately £102m requires funding solution
findings.detail: The cumulative budget gap from April 2027 to March 2030 is estimated at around £102m, driven by changes to the Government's funding formula and updated assumptions on pressures, commitments and funding. This gap will need to be addressed through the medium-term financial strategy and annual budget process.
findings.matters: A material multi-year budget deficit indicates significant financial stress that requires material savings or income-raising to balance, which is a key indicator of financial health for lenders
findings.figures: £102m cumulative over three financial years (April 2027 to March 2030)
findings.quote: the budget gap for the three financial years from April 2027 to March 2030 is estimated at around £102m, following changes to the Government's funding formula and updated assumptions on pressures, commitments and funding

findings.headline: Internal repairs service performance below target, indicating housing maintenance quality risk
findings.detail: The council's performance on internal repairs completed right first time was 79%, against a target of 90%. This is a material underperformance in a service that is critical to tenant satisfaction and property maintenance. The council holds the Mayor's Good Work Standard and is an accredited Living Wage employer, but housing maintenance performance is not tracking to standard.
findings.matters: Poor first-time fix rates on repairs suggest either understaffing, skills shortage, or resource constraint in the housing maintenance function. This can lead to tenant complaints, regulatory scrutiny, building safety concerns, and escalating maintenance backlogs that become more costly to resolve.
findings.figures: Internal repairs completed right first time 79%, target 90%, gap 11 percentage points
findings.quote: Internal repairs completed right first time 85% [target] 79% [actual] Below target

findings.headline: Social rent housing delivery fell significantly short of target (385 vs 579 target)
findings.detail: The council's performance table shows that social rent homes completed in 2025-26 were 385 against a target of 579, a shortfall of 194 homes. This is marked as 'Below target' performance. The council has committed to housing delivery and regeneration to meet the needs of its growing population, but this underperformance signals slippage in that priority.
findings.matters: Housing delivery shortfalls in a London borough with acute housing pressure and 307,600 residents signal either capital constraint, development delay, or planning friction. This matters to lenders assessing the council's capacity to deliver on its regeneration and housing supply commitments.
findings.figures: Social rent homes completed 385, target 579, shortfall 194
findings.quote: Social rent homes completed 579 [target] 385 [actual] Below target

findings.headline: High interest rates are constraining capital investment affordability
findings.detail: The document explicitly states that interest rates remained relatively high during 2025-26, increasing the cost of borrowing and placing pressure on the affordability of capital investment. This is noted as part of the external environment shaping the council's financial position.
findings.matters: High borrowing costs reduce the capital that the council can afford to spend on estates renewal, schools, infrastructure and housing. This compounds pressure on delivery of the council's regeneration and housing supply ambitions and extends payback periods for capital schemes.
findings.figures: No specific interest rate figures provided; borrowing affordability cited as pressured
findings.quote: Interest rates also remained relatively high, increasing the cost of borrowing and placing pressure on the affordability of capital investment.

findings.headline: Demand for temporary accommodation and social care remains unmatched by budgeted provision
findings.detail: The narrative states that housing affordability and homelessness remain significant local pressures, driving continued high demand for temporary accommodation services. Social care demand also remains elevated due to demographic pressures and increasingly complex needs. The document identifies these as continuing financial pressures reflected in the 2025-26 outturn and as key considerations for medium-term planning.
findings.matters: Demand-led services that are outrunning budget allocate scarce reserves and delay other capital and service investment. If demographic and housing market trends continue, the council faces compounding financial risk unless new funding sources or service models are found.
findings.figures: Temporary accommodation and social care cited as main drivers of £25.3m overspend
findings.quote: Housing affordability and the shortage of suitable accommodation remained significant local pressures, contributing to continued demand for homelessness services and temporary accommodation. Demand also remained high in adult and children's social care, reflecting demographic pressures and increasingly complex needs.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account in deficit of £1.4m from void properties and temporary accommodation use
findings.detail: The HRA, which funds the council's landlord function through rents and service charges, recorded a net deficit of £1.4m. The document cites reduced rental income caused by void properties and the use of homes for temporary accommodation as the main driver. Expenditure controls and stronger performance in some income streams only partly offset this. The HRA remains under pressure from these income losses, inflation, regulatory requirements and maintenance costs.
findings.matters: A deficit HRA signals that the council's housing stock is not self-financing. Void properties and use of stock for temporary accommodation represent a loss of planned income and a redirection of assets away from traditional landlord functions, affecting the HRA's medium-term sustainability.
findings.figures: HRA net deficit £1.4m for 2025-26
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the HRA continued to experience financial pressure, mainly from reduced rental income caused by void properties and the use of homes for temporary accommodation. The final HRA position was a net deficit of £1.4m.

findings.headline: General Fund overspend of £25.3m, driven by demand-led services and delayed savings delivery
findings.detail: The council budgeted £369.7m but spent £395m. The overspend was primarily driven by temporary accommodation and social care costs that exceeded forecasts. The document explicitly states delays in delivering planned transformation savings also contributed. The position was managed through reserve use and contingencies, but represents a deterioration compared to the previous year.
findings.matters: A £25.3m overspend on a £369.7m budget (6.8%) signals material delivery risk in the council's financial planning. Delayed savings indicate that transformation programmes are not tracking; this matters to lenders assessing the council's capacity to balance future budgets.
findings.figures: Net General Fund budget £369.7m, actual net expenditure £395m, adverse variance £25.3m
findings.quote: The final outturn showed net expenditure of £395m, resulting in an adverse variance of £25.3m. The main pressures were in demand-led services, particularly temporary accommodation and social care, alongside delays in delivering planned transformation savings.

findings.headline: CIPFA Financial Resilience Index flags comparatively higher-risk indicators on HRA long-term sustainability and external debt
findings.detail: The council completed the 2025 CIPFA Financial Resilience Index. While rated 'low risk' on overall financial sustainability and reserves, the assessment identified 'comparatively higher-risk indicators relating to the long-term sustainability of the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) and the level of external debt.' These are regularly reviewed but the index itself signals elevated risk in these two areas.
findings.matters: An external benchmarking tool flagging higher-risk indicators on HRA and debt levels is an independent warning sign. For a lender, a council with flagged debt and HRA sustainability risks requires closer monitoring of capital and borrowing plans.
findings.figures: HRA sustainability and external debt flagged as 'comparatively higher-risk indicators'
findings.quote: It also identified comparatively higher-risk indicators relating to the long-term sustainability of the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) and the level of external debt. These higher risk indicators are regularly considered alongside the council's Medium Term Financial Strategy, treasury management strategy and HRA recovery planning.

findings.headline: Internal audit opinion is 'generally satisfactory with improvements required in some areas'—below full assurance
findings.detail: The Chief Audit Executive's opinion for 2025-26 is 'Generally satisfactory with improvements required in some areas.' This means areas examined 'were found to be suitably designed and operating effectively to support the relevant risk management, control and governance arrangements, but that improvements are required in some areas to strengthen consistency and effectiveness across services.' This is not full assurance.
findings.matters: A qualified internal audit opinion, even at this moderate level, signals identified control weaknesses that have not yet been resolved. Lenders and finance directors need clarity on what those areas are and remediation timelines.
findings.figures: Overall opinion 2025-26: 'Generally satisfactory with improvements required in some areas'
findings.quote: For 2025–26, the overall opinion was 'Generally satisfactory with improvements required in some areas'. This means that the areas examined were found to be suitably designed and operating effectively to support the relevant risk management, control and governance arrangements, but that improvements are required in some areas to strengthen consistency and effectiveness across services.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review reduces Southwark's assessed funding need going forward; transitional protection ends 2028-29
findings.detail: The new funding formula 'results in a reduction in assessed relative need over the medium term, reflecting changes in national deprivation measures.' The council has a transitional protection package only through 2028-29. After that, the reduction in assessed need will feed directly into lower grant. The council has 'earmarked reserves to manage the transition' but this is a structural funding headwind.
findings.matters: A structural reduction in government funding (not a temporary freeze or delay) combined with short-term reserve-backed protection means the council faces a step-down in resources when the protection ends. For a lender, this signals declining future resources and potential pressure on long-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Reduction in assessed relative need confirmed; transitional protection to 2028-29 only
findings.quote: For Southwark, the new funding formula results in a reduction in assessed relative need over the medium term...The final settlement confirmed a three-year transitional protection package, including the Recovery Grant Guarantee, which protects the council at 100% of its 2025–26 funding baseline through to 2028–29.

findings.headline: HRA 2025-26 expected to show net overspend driven by repairs spend and rental income shortfall
findings.detail: The HRA outturn for 2025-26 'is expected to show a net overspend, driven mainly by repairs and maintenance due to increased spend on one of the housing estates in order to bring properties back into use and a shortfall in rental income.' This indicates both capital pressure (backlog of repairs) and operational revenue pressure (vacancies or collection issues).
findings.matters: Unplanned repairs spend on the housing estate and rental income shortfalls indicate asset condition problems and/or lettable quality issues. Both signal operational and revenue pressure on a £55,000-home portfolio.
findings.figures: Net overspend expected in 2025-26; repairs/maintenance increase plus rental income shortfall
findings.quote: The HRA outturn report will be considered by the Executive after this Audit, Governance and Standards Committee meeting and is expected to show a net overspend, driven mainly by repairs and maintenance due to increased spend on one of the housing estates in order to bring properties back into use and a shortfall in rental income

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation overspend exceeding £9.5m from prior year and rising in 2025-26
findings.detail: A £9.5m overspend in temporary accommodation was reported to Cabinet in June 2025. The statement explicitly flags that 'the 2025–26 outturn position is estimated to be higher than this.' The council attributes the ongoing pressure to the 'growing national homelessness crisis, unaffordable private rented accommodation, and restrictions on Local Housing Allowance.' Mitigations will continue into 2026-27.
findings.matters: A growing, uncontrolled demand pressure outside the council's direct control signals revenue volatility and ongoing budget stress. For a lender, unbudgeted demand-led overspends are a red flag for financial discipline.
findings.figures: £9.5m reported overspend (2024-25); 2025-26 outturn 'estimated to be higher than this'
findings.quote: the 2025–26 outturn position is estimated to be higher than this and will be reported to the Executive after this Audit, Governance and Standards Committee meeting

findings.headline: 2025-26 transformation savings target of £3m expected to deliver nothing materially
findings.detail: The council planned £3m of cashable transformation savings for 2025-26. The outturn report 'is expected to confirm that there is unlikely to be any material in-year savings delivered against the £3m target.' This cascades into a £10m requirement for 2026-27 (£7m planned plus the £3m shortfall), described as 'significant for delivery of the MTFS and the council's longer-term financial sustainability.'
findings.matters: Failing to deliver transformation savings—the core mechanism for achieving financial balance in the medium term—signals that the council's financial recovery depends on reserves or other measures. This is critical for a lender assessing financial resilience.
findings.figures: £3m expected zero delivery in 2025-26; £10m required for 2026-27 (£3m slippage plus £7m target)
findings.quote: it is expected to confirm that there is unlikely to be any material in-year savings delivered against the £3m target. As a result, the total savings requirement for 2026–27 increases to £10m, which is significant for delivery of the MTFS and the council's longer-term financial sustainability, including the potential for increased reliance on reserves.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account has £3.0m funding gap for 2026-27 after £5.25m of £8.25m savings identified
findings.detail: The HRA budget for 2026-27 requires £8.25m in savings to achieve balance, but only £5.25m had been identified as of April 2026. The council acknowledges 'the HRA remains under significant pressure and achieving balance depends on delivering further savings.' This follows a significant HRA deficit in 2023-24 and a recovery plan extended from 2025-26 into 2026-27.
findings.matters: A major social landlord (55,000 homes) unable to fully identify savings needed for balance in the medium term represents a sustainability risk. For a lender, unidentified savings gaps signal potential pressure on reserves or further borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: £8.25m total savings requirement for 2026-27; £5.25m identified; £3.0m gap
findings.quote: an assumed savings requirement of £8.25m (with £5.25m identified at the time, leaving a £3.0m gap). Despite progress, the HRA remains under significant pressure and achieving balance depends on delivering further savings.

findings.headline: No formal membership reconciliation process to verify accuracy of member records against payroll
findings.detail: The fund does not perform a formal annual reconciliation of membership changes or cross-check active and pensioner member records against underlying payroll data. This is a control weakness, though the fund is working to expand its membership reconciliation processes.
findings.matters: Inaccurate membership data could lead to overpayment of benefits or misstatement of pension liabilities, directly affecting the fund's financial position and future funding requirements.
findings.figures: Membership data forms basis for pension liability calculations in £2,261.94m fund
findings.quote: We noted that no formal member reconciliation is performed noting membership changes in the year, reconciling movements and cross checking against the underlying payroll records. There is a risk that membership information may be incorrect.

findings.headline: No formal management review or documented challenge of property valuations provided by external valuer
findings.detail: KPMG noted that while the fund engages Knight Frank (via Nuveen fund manager) to value the directly held property portfolio (£248.3m), there is no documented management review or challenge of these valuations. Auditing standards require a control meeting this requirement. The fund's view is that their approach adequately addresses risks, leaving this recommendation outstanding but closed.
findings.matters: Property represents 11% of pension fund assets. Without documented management challenge of valuations, there is reduced assurance that property values are accurate and not subject to systematic over- or under-valuation.
findings.figures: Directly held property valuation: £248.3m (11% of total assets)
findings.quote: Whilst the Audit, Governance and Standard Committee appoints a third-party fund manager, Nuveen to manage its property portfolio and who further in turn engage Knight Frank to value the property, we did not identify an associated management review or other control that meets the requirements of the auditing standards.

findings.headline: Control weakness: journal entries can be posted without enforced authorisation approval
findings.detail: The pension fund's SAP system is configured to require journal entry authorisation but does not technically enforce it, meaning entries could theoretically be posted without approval. While KPMG's testing found no unauthorised entries in practice, the system control is ineffective. The fund attributes this to system limitations and does not plan to remediate before SAP replacement.
findings.matters: Lack of enforced journal controls increases fraud risk and the risk of erroneous entries affecting the financial statements, particularly relevant given the scale of the pension fund's assets.
findings.figures: Total pension fund assets: £2,261.94m
findings.quote: We identified a weakness in journal entries because there are routes by which journal entries can be posted without authorisation or segregation of duties. This is typical of many large organisations, and the pension fund is satisfied it has adequate mitigations for the risks posed.

findings.headline: £1.6m uncorrected valuation overstatement in Level 3 pooled property funds due to lagged asset valuations
findings.detail: KPMG identified a £1.6m variance between the management's valuation recorded in the draft financial statements and more current valuations as at 31 March 2025 from investment managers. The issue arose because the fund was using quarterly valuation statements delayed by fund managers. KPMG assessed the resulting valuation as 'slightly optimistic as recorded.' The difference is immaterial individually but remains uncorrected.
findings.matters: Lagged valuations mean the fund's reported net asset position may not reflect actual current values, affecting decision-making for both lenders and the pension fund's own financial planning.
findings.figures: £1.6m overstatement; Level 3 pooled property investment vehicles total £413.51m (18% of £2,261.94m portfolio)
findings.quote: The draft financial statements are prepared on the basis of latest available valuations that are sometimes lagged due to a delay in preparing the quarterly valuation statements by investment managers. Our audit procedures involved obtaining valuations as at 31 March 2025. We have identified an overstatement of £1.60m between the values in the draft financial statements and those provided by the investment managers as at 31 March 2025.

findings.detail: Council reserves fell from £228.8m to £196.6m, a net reduction of £32.2m. findings.matters: Declining total reserves indicate the council is consuming its financial buffer to manage current year pressures rather than maintaining cushion for unexpected events or service demands, reducing resilience.

This rapid drawdown of a reserve intended to smooth demand volatility suggests cost pressures in this statutory service are exceeding budget and consuming the financial buffer.

findings.detail: Multiple major capital schemes are experiencing extended negotiations on final account settlements with contractors. findings.headline: Leisure decarbonisation programme represents cascading risk to dependent facility improvement works
findings.detail: Planned leisure facility improvement works and decarbonisation-related enabling works have been reprofiled from 2025-26 into 2026-27 to align with the wider Leisure Decarbonisation Programme. The council explicitly states that any changes or delays to the decarbonisation programme will have consequential impact on delivery of dependent improvement and enabling works.
findings.matters: Single-point-of-failure risk in capital delivery; decarbonisation programme delays will cascade to other council facilities and services, creating uncontrolled rescheduling risk

findings.detail: The traveller sites reconfiguration and improvement programme (focused on fire safety and health/safety compliance) experienced delivery failure: a previously appointed contractor at Ilderton Road was terminated after works were identified as delivered outside the approved legal framework. This caused programme delays. Procurement is now complete with majority of construction activity rescheduled for 2026-27.

findings.headline: Council provided £2.4m Strategic CIL subsidy to make BLE-compliant housing scheme developable
findings.detail: A 46-unit 100% affordable housing scheme at 634-636 Old Kent Road was paused when abnormal costs relating to Bakerloo Line Extension compliant foundation design proved unviable for the developer. Cabinet approved £2.37m Strategic CIL grant to Hexagon Housing Association to cover below-ground mitigation works required to future-proof the site against tunnel vibration and acoustic impacts, enabling the scheme to restart.
findings.matters: Council funding required to make externally-imposed infrastructure constraint economically viable for housing delivery; indicates strategic project cost burden passed to council
findings.figures: £2,373,563 Strategic CIL grant; 46 homes (8 social rent, 38 shared ownership); completion scheduled 2027-28
findings.quote: The development had been paused, because the abnormal cost relating to the BLE compliant design could not be viably borne by the development. The SCIL funding allocation supported the BLE compliant foundation in the development and therefore enabled the 46 homes (100% affordable) scheme to restart as per the original plan, with a scheduled completion in 2027/28.

findings.headline: Construction cost inflation and labour shortages driving capital programme constraints
findings.detail: The council identifies material ongoing pressures on capital delivery: labour shortage and skilled sub-contractor availability constraints, wage inflation outpacing general market growth, rising material costs from world markets and tariffs, and increased Building Control regime costs. Labour shortage is identified as the largest single concern, with wage inflation continuing to outstrip marketplace growth.
findings.matters: Inflationary cost pressures could require reprofiling, scope reductions, or additional funding across school, SEN and leisure capital schemes; may affect ability to deliver planned provision

findings.detail: The Local Authority Housing Fund Buyback 50 programme achieved only £5.7m of a £19.4m 2025-26 budget. findings.matters: Large variance from planned housing acquisition programme raises questions about delivery capacity and forecast accuracy; recovery depends on 2026-27 execution against a pattern of slippage

This variance reflects programme slippage and a decision to fund ten properties originally included in the programme through the Buy Back programme using Right to Buy receipts. The remaining slippage is expected to be recovered in 2026-27, when the programme will be completed.

findings.headline: Adult social care faces estimated £8m structural deficit without intervention
findings.detail: Children's and Adults' Services is experiencing sustained financial pressure from rising provider fees, inflationary cost increases, higher client need levels and complexity, delays in NHS treatment access, and hospital discharge pathways. Without intervention this creates an estimated £8m structural deficit. In-year action uses departmental resilience reserves to mitigate pressures, but this is not sustainable long-term.

findings.figures: £8m estimated structural deficit without intervention; use of departmental resilience reserves in 2025-26

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation overspend of £13.4m driven by structural demand and housing benefit subsidy gap
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation remains the primary area of overspend, reflecting national cost and demand pressures particularly severe in London. The council operates against an increased cost base due to continued reliance on higher-cost nightly paid accommodation following exits from the private leasing market. An additional £1.5m pressure arises from Housing Benefit subsidy loss where out-of-borough placement rates (Local Housing Allowance) are lower than Southwark costs. The council has limited influence over these market conditions.
findings.matters: TA identified by London councils as single biggest financial risk; external demand drivers (homelessness, landlord exits) not within council control; subsidy gap structural and unfunded
findings.figures: £13.4m overspend after mitigation; £1.5m Housing Benefit subsidy loss; improved from £15.6m forecast at month 6
findings.quote: London councils continue to identify temporary accommodation as the single biggest risk to London authority finances, driven by rising homelessness, landlords exiting borough arrangements, and the gap between housing benefit subsidy and actual cost. The outturn includes £1.5m relating to Housing Benefit subsidy loss arising from out-of-borough placements where Local Housing Allowance rates are lower than those in Southwark.

findings.headline: HRA rent-setting formula error discovered in temporary accommodation costing £8.3m
findings.detail: An incorrect application of the rent-setting formula in temporary accommodation was discovered, creating a £8.3m adverse cost pressure and requiring accounting adjustments for prior years. A £3.7m provision has been recognised for estimated refunds to current tenants. Additional contingent liability of £32.7m relating to former tenants and Housing Benefit subsidy including potential payments to DWP has been identified as uncertain.
findings.matters: Control failure in HRA charge-setting; unexpected liabilities discovered; contingent liability of £32.7m represents significant unquantified exposure; HRA already in poor financial position
findings.figures: £8.3m adverse variance 2025-26; £3.7m provision for tenant refunds; £32.7m contingent liability
findings.quote: In 2025-26, the discovery of the incorrect application of a rent-setting formula in temporary accommodation created a significant new cost pressure of £8.3m and knock-on effects on prior years through accounting adjustments. A provision of £3.7m has been recognised for estimated refunds to current tenants where repayment is considered probable. In addition, potential liabilities relating to former tenants and Housing Benefit subsidy, including payments to the DWP, have been assessed as uncertain and are therefore disclosed as a contingent liability estimated at £32.7m.

findings.headline: Transformation savings programme delivered only £80k against £3m 2025-26 target
findings.detail: The Future Southwark Transformation Programme achieved only £80k of the £3m savings target, resulting in a £2.9m adverse variance. Plans and business cases are in place for portions of this shortfall but timing has fallen behind schedule. The £7m target for 2026-27 is now being added to the £2.9m shortfall, creating a cumulative £10m challenge now pushed entirely into 2026-27.
findings.matters: Shows strategic transformation programme not executing; delayed delivery adds to budget pressures; further 2026-27 target at risk if underlying issues not resolved
findings.figures: £80k achieved vs £3m target in 2025-26; cumulative £10m savings now required in 2026-27
findings.quote: Delivery in 2025-26 was substantially below plan, with only £80k achieved against the £3m savings target, resulting in an adverse variance of £2.9m. findings.paper_title: Appendix Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 , item 12.
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review reduces council's assessed funding need with material risks once transitional protection ends
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review, implemented in 2025-26, resulted in a full reset of the business rates retention system. For Southwark, the new funding formula results in a reduction in assessed relative need over the medium term, reflecting changes in national deprivation measures and regeneration outcomes. A three-year transitional protection package protects the council at 100% of its 2025-26 funding baseline through 2028-29, but significant risks remain once this protection unwinds.
findings.matters: A structural reduction in government funding assessment compounds the council's existing structural pressures (HRA, temporary accommodation, savings delivery). Reliance on temporary protection that expires in 2029 means the council must resolve underlying affordability issues over the next three years.
findings.figures: Three-year transitional protection covering 100% of 2025-26 funding baseline through 2028-29; protection ends in 2029; MTFS extended to 2029-30; earmarked reserves set aside to manage transition
findings.quote: For Southwark, the new funding formula results in a reduction in assessed relative need over the medium term. The final settlement confirmed a three-year transitional protection package, which protects the council at 100% of its 2025–26 funding baseline through to 2028–29.

findings.paper_title: Appendix Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 , item 12.
findings.headline: Transformation savings programme failing to deliver, forcing £10m savings requirement into 2026-27
findings.detail: The council's Medium Term Financial Strategy included £3m transformation savings for 2025-26 and £7m for 2026-27. However, the 2025-26 outturn report is expected to confirm that there is unlikely to be any material in-year savings delivered against the £3m target. This failure cascades into 2026-27, creating a total savings requirement of £10m. The council states this is 'significant for delivery of the MTFS and the council's longer-term financial sustainability, including the potential for increased reliance on reserves'.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver planned savings indicates the council's transformation programme is not on track. A £10m savings gap in 2026-27 is material and suggests the council will rely on reserves rather than operational improvements, weakening underlying financial resilience.
findings.figures: £3m savings target 2025-26 (not achieved); £7m savings target 2026-27; combined £10m total requirement for 2026-27; separate mention of £10m transformation savings target by 2026-27
findings.quote: As a result, the total savings requirement for 2026–27 increases to £10m, which is significant for delivery of the MTFS and the council's longer-term financial sustainability, including the potential for increased reliance on reserves.

findings.paper_title: Appendix Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 , item 12.
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation overspend exceeds £9.5m baseline and is rising further in 2025-26
findings.detail: The council reported a £9.5m overspend in temporary accommodation at 31 March 2025, which was reported to Cabinet in June 2025. Despite establishment of a Temporary Accommodation Budget Recovery Board in 2025-26, the 2025-26 outturn position is estimated to be higher than the £9.5m baseline. The underlying drivers are structural: national homelessness crisis, unaffordable private rented sector, and Local Housing Allowance rates no longer covering private rental costs.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is highly demand-led and sensitive to national economic conditions. Persistent overspends above budget suggest the council cannot forecast or control this material cost, creating recurring year-on-year budget surprises and threatening MTFS assumptions.
findings.figures: £9.5m overspend at 31 March 2025; 2025-26 outturn estimated higher than £9.5m; £3m additional central government funding for homelessness prevention awarded for 2025-26 (but this appears insufficient to close gap)
findings.quote: The reported overspend of £9.5m as at 31 March 2025 was reported to Cabinet in June 2025. Despite this oversight, the 2025–26 outturn position is estimated to be higher than this and will be reported to the Executive after this Audit, Governance and Standards Committee meeting.

findings.paper_title: Appendix Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 , item 12.
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account continues to overspend despite recovery plan extended to 2026-27
findings.detail: The HRA entered a recovery plan following a significant deficit in 2023-24. The plan was extended from ending in 2025-26 to 2026-27. The 2025-26 outturn report is expected to show a net overspend driven by higher repairs and maintenance spending (particularly on one housing estate to bring properties back into use) and shortfalls in rental income. Pressures include unfunded regulatory costs from Fire Safety and Building Safety Acts, construction and energy inflation, and higher interest rates. For 2026-27, Cabinet approved a budget framework with an £8.25m savings requirement (only £5.25m identified, leaving a £3.0m gap).
findings.matters: The HRA represents material assets and borrowing on the council's balance sheet (55,000 homes). Continued overspends despite the recovery plan indicate structural affordability issues, not one-off problems, raising questions about the council's ability to service and maintain this housing stock sustainably.
findings.figures: £8.25m savings requirement 2026-27 (£5.25m identified, £3.0m shortfall); Phase 1 extended from 2025-26 to 2026-27; Phase 2 to rebuild reserves to £50m prudent target; 30-year HRA Business Plan being developed
findings.quote: Despite progress, the HRA remains under significant pressure and achieving balance depends on delivering further savings. Phase 2 of the Recovery Plan will coincide with a newly established 30-year HRA Business Plan and is expected to be presented to the Executive in line with the 2027–28 budget setting timetable.

findings.headline: The Future Southwark efficiency programme lacks a consolidated benefits realisation framework and has fragmented risk management, raising questions about whether targeted savings will be achieved
findings.detail: The audit found that while the programme has strong governance structures and documented plans, there is no programme-wide benefits realisation framework. findings.detail: The audit identified delays in referrals, weaknesses in waiting list auditing with no documented monitoring activity, and record-keeping gaps. The Occupational Therapy Team is not completing monthly waiting list reporting, and the Assessment & Intake Team's PowerBI reporting lacks required detail on average waiting times and delays.

findings.detail: The council's critical social care management system has not received a full application upgrade in approximately one year (planned upgrades delayed). User accounts for staff leavers remain active after their departure, with no formal process to review access when staff change roles. Data quality issues including duplicate, incomplete and historic records have been identified but the cleansing programme is not yet fully implemented. Several users retain ability to apply or amend restricted record permissions with no documented rationale or end dates.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about the integrity of the data underpinning the council's assessment of social care needs, costs, and service delivery. System control weaknesses create risks of fraud, error, and safeguarding failures.

findings.paper_title: Report: Setting the council tax 2026-27 , item 2.2
findings.headline: Net revenue budget increased 18% in one year to £420.4m, drivers not explained in this document
findings.detail: The net revenue budget has risen from £356.4m in 2025-26 to £420.4m in 2026-27, an increase of £63.9m or 18%. The report does not explain the drivers of this significant increase, stating only that detail is in the related Policy and Resources Strategy report.
findings.matters: An 18% year-on-year budget increase is substantial and would typically indicate significant cost growth or new commitments that require investigation to assess sustainability and underlying financial pressures.
findings.quote: The proposed net revenue budget for Southwark council is £420,386,806

findings.paper_title: Report: Setting the council tax 2026-27 , item 2.2
findings.headline: Adult social care precept has been repeatedly maximised, reaching 22% cumulative increase over ten years
findings.detail: The council has applied the maximum available adult social care precept for 2026-27 at 2.00%, continuing a pattern of consistent maximisation. From 2016-17 to 2026-27, the cumulative ASC precept has increased by 22%, totalling £245.00 on band D. This shows sustained structural funding pressure in adult social care.
findings.matters: Repeated maximisation of the adult social care precept demonstrates structural funding pressures that cannot be addressed through council tax alone, signalling ongoing service strain and potential future sustainability challenges.
findings.figures: 22% cumulative increase from 2016-17 to 2026-27 totalling £245.00; 2% increase in 2026-27 equalling £27.75
findings.quote: The council has maximised its usage of the adult social care precept with a cumulative 22% increase from 2016-17 to 2026-27 totalling £245.00

findings.paper_title: Report: Setting the council tax 2026-27 , item 2.2
findings.headline: Southwark is setting council tax at the maximum increase permitted without a referendum
findings.detail: The council is increasing the Southwark element of council tax by 4.99% (2.00% adult social care precept plus 2.99% local increase), which equals the maximum local council tax increase permitted without breaching the government's 5.00% referendum cap. This indicates the council has used all available tax-raising headroom.
findings.matters: Maxing out the allowed tax increase signals that a council has exhausted its primary tool for raising local revenue without referendum, indicating significant budget pressure and limited remaining options.
findings.figures: 4.99% increase at the 5.00% referendum cap limit
findings.quote: being the maximum local council tax increase permitted without breaching the government referendum cap of 5.00%

findings.detail: The June 2025 Spending Review confirmed no additional capital funding beyond existing allocations for decarbonisation or building safety programmes. The council must fund these statutory obligations (Building and Fire Safety Acts, Awaab's Law on damp/mould) from rental income.
findings.matters: A lender funding the HRA needs to understand that capital investment in building safety and legal compliance cannot be deferred and must compete with base service funding, creating potential trade-offs between service quality and capital investment.

findings.quote: The Spending Review also confirmed that no additional capital funding would be made available to support decarbonisation or building safety programmes beyond existing allocations, placing further reliance on rental income to sustain investment in the housing stock.

findings.headline: Rent convergence policy details delayed to January 2026 creates planning uncertainty for HRA income of £1.7m–£5.1m annually
findings.detail: Government consultation on social rent convergence was expected in the Autumn Statement (26 November 2025) but has been delayed to January 2026. Approximately 33,600 tenanted properties remain below formula rent. Depending on the uplift mechanism (£1, £2, or £3 weekly), this could generate £1.7m, £3.4m, or £5.1m in additional annual income, but neither the mechanism nor the timeline is confirmed.
findings.matters: A material swing in HRA income (potentially £5.1m+) remains unquantified three months before the new financial year begins, creating budget execution risk and uncertainty about the sustainability of service improvement commitments.
findings.figures: 33,600 properties below formula rent; potential additional income of £1.7m, £3.4m, or £5.1m depending on weekly uplift (£1, £2, or £3)
findings.quote: Based on current estimates, approximately 33,600 tenanted properties remain below formula rent (target). Applying a £1, £2, or £3 weekly uplift to these properties would generate an additional £1.7m, £3.4m, or £5.1m respectively in annual HRA income.
