findings.headline: Cumulative loss of over £1bn from past rent policy caps constrains HRA financial position over 30-year plan
findings.detail: The council has suffered two major periods of rent policy intervention: a 1% annual rent reduction from 2016-2020 and a 7% cap in 2023-24. These interventions have created a cumulative shortfall estimated to exceed £1bn over the 30-year HRA business plan, with no government compensation for lost income despite the new 10-year CPI+1% certainty.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the HRA's long-term financial sustainability needs to understand this structural underfunding and whether the current rent policy can close the gap, particularly given competing capital demands from building safety and damp/mould obligations.
findings.figures: Cumulative impact estimated to exceed £1bn over 30-year business plan; 7% rent cap in 2023-24 created loss of c.£9m+ per annum
findings.quote: Southwark's HRA continues to endure significant financial pressure, with the cumulative impact of past interventions estimated to exceed £1bn over the life of the 30-year business plan.

findings.headline: Pension fund has no documented management review process for £248.3m directly held property portfolio
findings.detail: The fund holds £248.3m in directly held property (11% of total assets), valued entirely by external valuer Knight Frank via fund manager Nuveen. Auditors found that while management assessed the valuation as appropriate, the review "was not performed on a sufficiently detailed or documented basis to allow us to rely on the control." Consequently, auditors concluded that controls over this significant asset class were ineffective. KPMG identified this as a Priority 2 control deficiency requiring attention.
findings.matters: A substantial asset class with significant valuation uncertainty is reviewed without documented internal scrutiny or challenge process, creating single-point-of-failure reliance on the external valuer and potential for undetected valuation errors.
findings.figures: £248.3m directly held property; represents 11% of £2,261.94m total fund
findings.quote: Directly held property valuation is assessed by management for appropriateness. However, the review was not performed on a sufficiently detailed or documented basis to allow us to rely on the control. Consequently, we concluded that controls in place to review the valuation were ineffective, consistent with the prior period.

findings.headline: Pension fund initially overstated Level 3 pooled investments by £1.6m using lagged valuations
findings.detail: The draft financial statements recorded pooled property valuations at the latest available date rather than 31 March 2025 year-end. During audit, KPMG obtained current confirmations from fund managers and identified a £1.6m variance between management's recorded value and the actual year-end NAV, primarily relating to Invesco holdings. Auditors assessed the valuation as slightly optimistic. While not material to the audit opinion, this indicates the fund's valuation process used stale pricing data.
findings.matters: Overstated investment valuations can lead to inaccurate assessment of the pension fund's solvency position and may result in incorrect contribution rate setting, potentially creating unfunded liabilities the council must cover.
findings.figures: £1.6m overstatement; £2,261.94m total net assets at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: We have identified an overstatement of £1.60m between the values in the draft financial statements and those provided by the investment managers as at 31 March 2025. This is relating to Invesco. This is not material to our financial statement's opinion, but we do consider the valuation to be slightly optimistic as recorded.

findings.headline: Community Municipal Investment scheme plans for 2026-27 remain under review
findings.detail: The council has raised £2.5m through Community Municipal Investments (crowdfunding) to date but has not committed to continuing or expanding the scheme in 2026-27, pending assessment of how previous schemes performed.
findings.matters: Alternative funding source remains unproven and uncertain for the upcoming year; unclear commitment affects available capital financing flexibility.
findings.figures: £2.5m to date; 2026-27 plans pending
findings.quote: To date £2.5m has been raised via this route plans for 2026-27 are under review pending assessment of the previous schemes.

findings.headline: Capital strategy undergoing review for CIPFA alignment; revised version due February 2026
findings.detail: External consultants have reviewed the capital strategy; officers are currently updating it to better align with CIPFA guidance on asset management, strategy linkages, and staff training, with the updated strategy due for Council Assembly approval in February.
findings.matters: Suggests prior misalignment in capital strategy governance requiring correction; impacts capital planning, asset management and control frameworks.
findings.figures: February 2026 approval deadline
findings.quote: Following a review by external consultants, officers are currently updating the capital strategy so that is better aligned with CIPFA guidance in areas such as links to other key strategies, council priorities, and asset management.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing from £1.85bn to £2.2bn over four years
findings.detail: The underlying capital financing requirement—the council's borrowing need for capital investment—is forecast to grow £350m from £1.85bn (2024-25 actual) to £2.2bn (2028-29), reflecting expanding capital commitments across the medium term.
findings.matters: Rising capital financing needs drive borrowing requirements and revenue pressures; indicates expanding asset-based obligations and longer-term debt profile.
findings.figures: £1.85bn (2024-25 actual) increasing to £2.2bn (2028-29)
findings.quote: Capital Finance Requirement 1,850 2,246 1,970 2,070 2,110 2,200

findings.headline: Council forecasts £145m in new borrowing required for 2026-27
findings.detail: The forecasted borrowing requirement for 2026-27 is estimated at £145m (period 44 monitor), representing the scale of external debt the council plans to issue to fund capital investment.
findings.matters: Quantifies annual new debt issuance and its revenue budget impact through debt servicing costs; identifies material reliance on capital markets.
findings.quote: For 2026-27 the forecasted borrowing requirement is currently estimated to be £145m (period 44 monitor).

findings.headline: Elevated borrowing costs are challenging the affordability of the council's capital programme
findings.detail: The paper notes that borrowing costs have risen significantly since the capital programme's inception and forecasts indicate they will remain elevated throughout 2026-27 and the medium term. The council explicitly identifies that higher borrowing rates put pressure on revenue budgets, reducing the resources available for additional borrowing, which it says challenges the affordability of the capital programme.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can sustain its capital investment commitments at current cost levels. If affordability is genuinely challenged, the council may need to defer, scale back, or refinance projects, affecting its ability to service debt.
findings.figures: £145 million borrowing requirement for 2026-27; net borrowing forecast to rise from £1,106m (2025) to £1,602m (2030); base rate forecast to fall only to 3.75% by end of 2025
findings.quote: Elevated borrowing rates put pressure on these budgets as less resources are available to take additional borrowing and this challenges the affordability of the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Year End Audit Report Council
findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing issued damning judgment with concerns; Council has developed action plan but implementation not yet tested
findings.detail: The Council received a damning judgment from the Regulator of Social Housing raising several concerns. While KPMG found the Council has developed an action plan to rectify the RSH issues with relevant actions and appropriate governance, this is a first test — the arrangements have not yet been implemented or demonstrated to be effective.
findings.matters: RSH intervention signals service quality failures affecting residents. Future RSH penalties are possible if the action plan fails. Housing service deterioration affects both council reputation and potentially housing revenue account finances.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided; RSH judgment made during 2024/25
findings.quote: During 2024/25, the Council received a damning judgement from the Regulator of Social Housing, raising several concerns... However, if the Council does not have an adequately governed arrangement to improve its housing service, there is a risk of future penalty by the RSH, as well as a worsening quality of service for Southwark residents.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Year End Audit Report Council
findings.headline: Audit incomplete pending objection resolution; value for money conclusions may vary from those reported
findings.detail: An objection to the accounts has been received and accepted. This prevents KPMG from reaching final value for money conclusions. Specifically, work in respect of the objection prevents certification of the audit. The audit report notes that VFM conclusions may vary from those reported in the current document when the Audit Completion Certificate is issued (anticipated early 2026).
findings.matters: An open objection creates uncertainty about the final audit conclusions. Unresolved challenges to the accounts suggest contested financial positions or governance failures that remain under investigation.
findings.figures: Anticipated Audit Completion Certificate issuance in early 2026; current report is draft
findings.quote: An element of the objection received prevents us from reaching our final value for money conclusions. Consequently our value for money conclusions may vary from those reported in this document when we issue our Audit Completion Certificate, anticipated in early 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Year End Audit Report Council
findings.headline: Pension liability assumptions assessed as optimistic; asset ceiling restricts net pension asset to £nil
findings.detail: The Southwark Local Government Pension Scheme net pension surplus has been restricted to £nil on the basis of estimated future service costs less estimated minimum funding contributions. KPMG found the assumptions used in valuing the defined benefit obligation to be optimistic compared to actuarial benchmarks but within acceptable range. However, actuarial review by management was not performed on a sufficiently detailed or documented basis to be relied upon.
findings.matters: Pension asset ceilings represent a significant balance sheet risk if funding valuations improve. The council is currently preventing any surplus recognition, masking the true economic pension position. Weak review controls over actuarial assumptions increase restatement risk.
findings.figures: Net LGPS surplus restricted to £nil; gross LGPS assets £1,590m (down £238m year-on-year); liabilities £1,590m
findings.quote: The net pension surplus has been restricted to £nil on the basis of estimated future service costs less the estimated minimum funding contributions meaning the surplus is not recoverable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Year End Audit Report Council
findings.headline: Weak controls over journal entries including over-privileged user access to general ledger system
findings.detail: KPMG identified weaknesses in the control environment for journal entries, including over-privileged user access to the general ledger system. The system allows journal entries to be posted without authorisation or segregation of duties. While common across large organisations, this is a documented control deficiency.
findings.matters: Journal entry controls are a baseline fraud prevention measure. Weak controls mean management override of accounts is possible without detection, which is particularly relevant given this is a mandatory fraud risk assessment area.
findings.figures: 22 high-risk journal entries identified in testing; no inappropriate entries found to date but testing incomplete
findings.quote: We have also identified weaknesses in the control environment for journal entries, including over-privileged user access to the Council's general ledger system.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Year End Audit Report Council
findings.headline: £9m uncorrected accrual for backdated pension contributions where no accounting obligation existed at balance sheet date
findings.detail: The Council created an accrual to pay backdated pension contributions to staff who were erroneously not auto-enrolled into the LGPS. However, KPMG identified that the Council did not have an accounting obligation to do so at the balance sheet date because it had not yet informed the affected staff. This is an uncorrected factual misstatement of £9m.
findings.matters: This represents an unquantified future liability for which the Council has provisioned £9m without a triggering event. If similar unidentified auto-enrolment failures exist, the total exposure could be materially higher.
findings.figures: £9m uncorrected misstatement (factual classification)
findings.quote: The Council has created an accrual to pay backdated pension contributions to staff who were erroneously not auto-enrolled into the LGPS. However, the Council did not have an accounting obligation to do so at the balance sheet date as it had not yet informed the affected staff.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Year End Audit Report Council
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account sustainability uncertain; stock condition survey underway with risk of material repair backlog
findings.detail: The Council has taken action to rebuild HRA financial sustainability but work remains to ensure it generates recurrent surpluses. A stock condition survey has been commissioned but is still in early stages. Initial trial feedback identified five severe HHSRS failures which reduced Decent Homes Standard compliance by 7%. As of end October (one month into full programme), 79 severe failures and 22 moderate failures identified. Costs for remedial action are significant but not yet quantified.
findings.matters: A material repair backlog could undermine the recent improvements in HRA finances. The Council is still uncertain of the full cost impact on the HRA, which could require significant additional borrowing or reserves drawdown to address compliance failures.
findings.figures: 79 Category 1 (severe) failures and 22 Category 2 (moderate) failures identified in first month; pilot phase identified 5 severe failures reducing compliance by 7%
findings.quote: The most pressing remaining action is in relation to stock condition, due to the risk that there is a material backlog of repair works required to bring homes to a decent standard.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Year End Audit Report Council
findings.headline: Major works schemes (Devon Mansions, Canada Estate) had substantial systematic control weaknesses in contract management
findings.detail: KPMG identified a significant VFM risk that the Council may not have appropriate arrangements in place in relation to managing contracts for major works. A detailed review into two major works schemes identified substantial systematic weaknesses in controls regarding contract management, with realistic risk that the Council systematically does not have appropriate governance arrangements or arrangements to ensure capital investment is done economically, efficiently and effectively.
findings.matters: Major works are significant capital commitments. Systematic governance failures in contract management can lead to cost overruns, delays, and poor value for money. This is particularly material given the Council's large housing stock and capital programme.
findings.figures: Concerns raised about multi-million pound schemes; specific schemes named are Devon Mansions and Canada Estate
findings.quote: After year-end, we became aware of a detailed review into two major works that took place during the year which identified substantial systematic weaknesses in controls in respect of major works schemes, where there is a realistic risk that the Council systematically does not have appropriate governance arrangements in relation to contract management

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Year End Audit Report Council
findings.headline: £4.5m investment property understatement corrected; valuation not supported by market evidence
findings.detail: KPMG identified one investment property where the valuation was not in line with available market evidence, resulting in an understatement of £4.5m that was corrected. The Council's investment property portfolio is £303m and includes commercial units and a large real estate scheme near the Council offices in London Bridge.
findings.matters: Commercial property valuations are inherently uncertain but market-based. A £4.5m error on a single asset suggests valuation processes did not adequately verify against current market conditions, particularly relevant given heightened uncertainty in commercial office markets.
findings.figures: £4.5m understatement; investment property portfolio £303m total (up £13m year-on-year)
findings.quote: The value of one investment property could not be supported by market comparatives. We therefore believe the valuation of this investment property was incorrect.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Year End Audit Report Council
findings.headline: £29m understatement of council dwellings valuation due to beacon group calculation error
findings.detail: An input error in the valuation of one beacon meant that the incorrect value was recorded for approximately 700 assets. KPMG identified a corrected factual £29m understatement of the valuation due to an error in the application of valuation judgements. The error could have been avoided through more rigorous review prior to recording in the financial statements.
findings.matters: This represents a material misstatement in the council's largest asset class (£3.6bn housing stock). Weak valuation controls allowed a systematic error affecting 700 properties to reach the accounts, raising questions about the robustness of the asset base.
findings.figures: £29m understatement across ~700 dwellings; council dwellings total £3,572m (up £180m year-on-year)
findings.quote: When extrapolated across the beacon group, a factual £29m understatement of the value of dwellings was identified. This error could have been avoided through a more rigorous review and assessment of the valuations prior to recording within the financial statements.

findings.headline: Cyber security and IT resilience risk is high (score 89) with internal audit actions still pending
findings.detail: The register identifies 'Total or partial loss of significant core business systems, inadequate data security' as a material risk with a raw score of 89 (controlled to 78). Notably, the assurance commentary states 'Internal Audit – 2 remaining audit actions pending', indicating incomplete remediation of identified weaknesses.
findings.matters: Unresolved IT audit actions indicate control gaps; a major cyber incident or system failure could disrupt financial reporting, payroll, and revenue collection, threatening operational continuity.
findings.figures: Risk score 89 (raw) to 78 (controlled); 2 internal audit actions pending
findings.quote: Internal Audit – 2 remaining audit actions pending.

findings.headline: School deficits have been significantly reduced but coupled with surplus primary places, creating ongoing budget pressure
findings.detail: School deficits and surplus places in primary schools are flagged as a red/amber risk (raw score 88, controlled 29). The council reports 'we have more than halved the number of schools in financial deficit and our strategy continues despite headwinds'. However, the risk remains active due to 'rising numbers of surplus places in primary schools' and ongoing 'pressure on school budgets and ultimately council budgets'.
findings.matters: School deficits are a leading indicator of budget stress across a council's entire education and social services portfolio; surplus capacity signals demographic challenges and future unfunded costs.
findings.figures: Risk score reduced from 88 to 29; more than half the number of schools in deficit have been resolved
findings.quote: School deficit balances coupled with the challenge of rising numbers of surplus places in primary schools creates pressure on school budgets and ultimately council budgets

findings.headline: Hundreds or thousands of ESA claimants face homelessness or destitution if they fail to migrate to Universal Credit
findings.detail: The register flags that government welfare reforms (Move to UC) create 'risks for vulnerable households (the ESA cohort) with an unknown number (potentially hundreds or thousands) at risk of failing to migrate successfully to UC and destitution or homelessness'. This is identified as part of the cost-of-living crisis and socio-economic risk.
findings.matters: A large cohort at risk of homelessness will create sudden, unbudgeted spikes in emergency support and TA costs; this is an identifiable but unquantified liability.
findings.figures: Unknown number, potentially hundreds or thousands
findings.quote: Government welfare reforms such as Move to UC create risks for vulnerable households (the ESA cohort) with an unknown number (potentially hundreds or thousands) at risk of failing to migrate successfully to UC and destitution or homelessness.

findings.headline: Medium-term financial strategy is not sufficiently robust against interest rate volatility and unclear future government funding
findings.detail: The register identifies future budgets (General Fund and HRA) as not sufficiently robust, with a raw risk score of 88. The council has a 3-year approved budget through 2026/27 and is lobbying government for funding clarity, but the register notes 'The confirmed outcome of future government reforms may affect the risk profile'—indicating material uncertainty about the financial landscape.
findings.matters: Weak medium-term financial planning indicates a council exposed to funding shocks and unable to forecast its fiscal position with confidence; this directly affects creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Risk score 88 (raw) to 69 (controlled)
findings.quote: Future budgets (General Fund and HRA) for the council are not sufficiently robust, especially in light of the current economic climate e.g. interest rate volatility and future local government funding changes

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation costs are rising with limited early-stage mitigation and medium-level assurance
findings.detail: TA is flagged as an amber/red risk (score 82 raw, 67 controlled) due to increasing supply pressures to tackle homelessness. The register notes that 'some mitigations are at an early stage, e.g. Training on landlord and tenant law, which limits current assurance' and recommends 'introducing KPIs to track the reduction in the use of TA could improve the operational assessment'.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation costs are a major and volatile budget driver for councils; rising demand without matched funding creates uncontrollable service overspends.
findings.figures: Risk score 82 (raw) to 67 (controlled); assessment of assurance is medium
findings.quote: Level of Assurance is medium. Some mitigations are at an early stage, e.g. Training on landlord and tenant law, which limits current assurance. Introducing KPIs to track the reduction in the use of TA could improve the operational assessment.

findings.headline: Council tax collection remains below pre-pandemic levels, constraining income in a cost-of-living crisis
findings.detail: The risk register notes explicitly that council tax collection has not recovered to pre-pandemic 2019-20 levels. The council is implementing a consistent approach to council tax debt write-off and running a SIIP CTAX debt project, but the register identifies stagnant or falling living standards and government consultation on CTAX collection arrangements as ongoing risks.
findings.matters: Council tax is a stable, predictable income source; a structural shortfall in collection signals weaker repayment capacity and households under financial stress.
findings.figures: Council tax collection below 2019-20 pre-pandemic baseline
findings.quote: Council tax collection has not recovered to pre-pandemic (2019-20 levels)

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account overspends threaten to deplete housing reserves and prevent balanced budgets
findings.detail: The risk register identifies HRA overspends on revenue and capital accounts as a material threat to housing reserves. The council has created recovery plans and refreshed its capital investment programme, but the controlled risk score of 69 indicates significant ongoing concern. The council is pursuing a development agreement model to minimise costs to the council.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion directly constrains a council's financial flexibility and ability to fund capital programmes; lenders track reserve adequacy as a key solvency indicator.
findings.figures: Risk score 82 (raw) reduced to 69 (controlled)
findings.quote: Overspends on the housing revenue and capital accounts result in the depletion of housing reserves resulting in an inability to set a balanced revenue budget or deliver on the council's housing investment programme.

findings.headline: Funding reform poses risk to financial sustainability; medium-term financial plan shows no unidentified savings but excludes funding reform impact
findings.detail: The Council's refreshed medium-term financial strategy (2024-25 to 2026-27) shows no unidentified savings required (down from £11m in February 2024), but this excludes potential impact of government funding reform. The paper notes London Boroughs are forecast to see the largest funding losses while facing significant financial pressure.
findings.matters: Funding reform is a known external shock that the MTFS does not yet quantify. A lender needs to understand the Council's stress-test assumptions and contingency plans if grant reductions are larger or faster than anticipated.
findings.figures: No unidentified savings in MTFS (down from £11m in prior year); impact of funding reform unknown
findings.quote: although this excludes the potential impact of funding reform on the Council's finances as they were unknown at the time of preparing the MTFS.

findings.headline: Finance system so old it enforces antiquated working practices; replacement critical to achieving transformation savings
findings.detail: The Council has flagged that its finance system is outdated and enforces inefficient working practices. An upgrade and replacement programme is underway as a key plank of the Council's transformation programme. The auditor notes that achievement of these savings is essential for long-term financial sustainability.
findings.matters: A decade-old finance system that impedes efficiency is a drag on savings delivery. For a lender, this signals that efficiency improvements will require upfront capital investment and carry execution risk.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: the upgrade and replacement of its finance system, as the age of the system enforces antiquated and inefficient working practices. Achievement of these savings will be essential in ensuring the Council remains financially sustainable following anticipated reductions in grants following planned changes to how local government is funded.

findings.headline: TMO governance weakness re-identified: one TMO misappropriated cyclical decoration funds; eight TMOs now in poor financial health
findings.detail: A prior-period weakness in TMO oversight has resurfaced. Fair Community Housing Services TMO spent funds intended for cyclical decorations on other activities; the TMO was deregistered for non-compliance. The Council has now identified eight TMOs in poor financial health with insufficient reserves to either complete committed cyclical works or return funds. Governance arrangements are new and still embedding.
findings.matters: TMO mismanagement is a proxy for weak leaseholder/tenant governance and emerging liability. If cyclical works are not completed, the Council—as freeholder—may face legal claims or forced spending to remediate. This is an operational and financial risk.
findings.figures: Eight TMOs identified in poor financial health; cyclical decorations recovery incomplete
findings.quote: the TMO was found to have spent funds intended for cyclical decorations on other activities. An action plan was developed to prevent similar issues occurring in the future, however we could not identify sufficiently developed governance arrangements to ensure those actions were implemented.

findings.headline: Governance issues escalated from 2 to 4 in one year; RSH inspection, TMO failures, and cyber risk now flagged
findings.detail: The Council reported four governance issues in 2024-25 (vs. two in 2023-24): RSH regulatory inspection, TMO governance breakdown, school financial sustainability, cyber security, and ERP replacement programme. The auditor has identified these as emerging risks that require active management.
findings.matters: A doubling of governance issues in one year signals loss of control and emerging operational risk. For a lender, this suggests stretched management bandwidth and heightened risk of further deterioration if not addressed.
findings.figures: 4 governance issues (2024-25) vs 2 (2023-24)
findings.quote: 4 issues identified, relating to: RSH regulatory inspection; TMO governance; school financial sustainability; cyber security; and ERP replacement programme.

findings.headline: Procurement rules breached on major works by 50-75% on scheme values; investigation ongoing
findings.detail: On Devon Mansions and Canada Estate schemes, the Council awarded contracts that exceeded their approved procurement values by 50-75% and breached its own contract extension procedures. A review identified the breaches; forensic review found no fraud but raised questions about governance. An objection to the 2024-25 accounts has been lodged. Investigation is ongoing and conclusions will be reported separately.
findings.matters: Procurement breaches of this magnitude indicate weak internal controls and oversight. If the Council is not policing its own rules on large capital works, value-for-money and fraud risk both increase. A lender needs to understand the root cause and remediation plan.
findings.figures: Value overruns 50-75% on individual schemes (not totaled in paper)
findings.quote: the value of these schemes exceeded the values approved as part of the procurement exercise of around 50-75% depending on the scheme, and the Council's arrangements for contract extensions were not followed.

findings.headline: 30% of council homes do not meet decent homes standard and no current stock condition survey in place
findings.detail: The RSH identified that roughly 30% of the Council's housing stock fails to meet the statutory Decent Homes Standard. The Council lacks a current stock condition survey, so the true scale of remediation work is unknown. A pilot survey was conducted but full results are pending. This is a material liability with no clear price tag.
findings.matters: Unquantified maintenance backlogs create contingent liabilities and future budget pressure. The Council cannot plan or budget properly without knowing the true state of its largest asset. This is a financial sustainability risk.
findings.figures: c. 30% of homes not meeting decent homes standard; exact proportion unknown
findings.quote: the Council has identified that a significant proportion of homes (c. 30%) are not meeting the decent homes standard although the exact proportion in this condition is unknown due to a lack of an up to date stock condition survey.

findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing downgraded Council to C3 (non-compliant) for failing consumer duty
findings.detail: The Regulator issued a C3 rating reflecting lack of electrical safety tests, a large proportion of homes non-decent, unfair housing allocation policy, and weak TMO governance. C3 is a non-compliant grading. The RSH declined to take enforcement action pending Council's corrective action, but made clear that non-compliance will trigger enforcement if not remedied.
findings.matters: Regulatory sanctions against the housing function are rare and serious. They signal operational and governance failure at scale. For a lender, this raises questions about management capability and the cost of remediation.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: the Regulator of Social Housing (RSH) issued the Council with a C3 rating in respect of the Council's compliance with the regulator's Consumer Duty.

findings.headline: General fund reserves fell by £11m and are now under downward pressure from housing and social care
findings.detail: The general fund reserve fell £11m in 2024-25 (reversing a £32m increase the prior year). The trajectory is worsening. The auditor notes the Council has ample buffer to respond to unexpected pressures but warns that reserves will need to be built back through achieving transformation savings, especially given risk of funding reductions.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion at this rate, if sustained, limits the Council's shock-absorbing capacity and its ability to invest in transformation. A lender needs visibility of the Council's plan to stabilise or rebuild reserves.
findings.figures: General fund balance fell £11m in 2024-25 (vs increase of £32m in 2023-24)
findings.quote: the Council's overall general fund balance fell by £11m during 2024-25 (£32m increase during 2023-24).

findings.headline: General fund overspent by £18m and contingency use more than tripled year-on-year
findings.detail: 2024-25 outturn was £373m against budget of £355m. The £18m shortfall was driven primarily by temporary accommodation demand exceeding budget. Contingency funds used jumped from £1.4m to £5.3m. While low as a percentage of outturn, the three-fold increase signals mounting pressure.
findings.matters: Escalating contingency draw indicates the Council is struggling to forecast and control demand-led spending, particularly in homelessness. This is a structural problem, not a one-off, and presages future budget shortfalls.
findings.figures: Budget £355m, outturn £373m, overspend £18m; contingency use £5.3m (vs £1.4m prior year)
findings.quote: the Council was required to use £5.3m of contingency funds, an increase from £1.4m in the prior period.

findings.headline: New homes programme curtailed because high interest rates make it unfinancial
findings.detail: The Council has deliberately scaled back its housebuilding programme because borrowing from PWLB at current rates is no longer cost-justified. It is exploring alternative delivery models including purchasing homes from developers rather than building them, and negotiating with central government.
findings.matters: This signals how interest rates are constraining capital strategy. For a lender, it demonstrates the Council's sensitivity to borrowing costs and willingness to abandon strategic priorities when financing becomes too expensive.
findings.figures: Not quantified in paper
findings.quote: the Council has been pairing back its new homes programme as it is not considered financially viable. The Council is looking at alternative delivery models to build new homes, such as purchasing social homes from developers building housing estates, and is exploring how it could work with central Government to fulfil its housebuilding ambitions.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account reserve too small for council of this size and HRA borrowing is now funding capital works
findings.detail: The HRA reserve sits at £21m, assessed as small. The Council has started borrowing to fund capital investment in homes—a shift driven by inability to generate operating surpluses. This compounds financial sustainability challenges and creates additional interest costs. The HRA recovery plan's first-year surplus included non-recurrent factors, creating risk of deficits re-emerging.
findings.matters: Growing HRA deficits and resort to borrowing signal deteriorating housing finances. A lender needs to understand whether the Council can service housing debt or will require general-fund bailouts.
findings.figures: HRA reserve £21m (increased £4m from 2023-24); HRA surplus 2024-25 £3.9m (vs deficit £2.5m prior year)
findings.quote: the HRA reserve sits at £21m which is considered small for a Council of this size. However, it is an increase of £4m since 2023-24... the Council has now started to borrow to fund capital investment.

findings.headline: 2026-27 budget will be shaped by government proposals on rent convergence, announcement deferred to autumn 2026
findings.detail: The council's budget-setting process for 2026-27 will be influenced by government proposals on the reintroduction of rent convergence. The announcement is scheduled for the Autumn statement in 2026, leaving budget planning uncertain until then.
findings.matters: Rent convergence could materially increase or constrain HRA income; the deferral of this decision creates planning uncertainty and may delay resolution of structural budget pressures.
findings.figures: Not quantified; announcement deferred to autumn 2026
findings.quote: will be influenced by government proposals on the reintroduction of rent convergence, which will be announced in the Autumn statement on 26 November 2026.

findings.headline: Recovery plan phase 2 targets reserve rebuild to £50 million and restriction of new borrowing
findings.detail: The council is implementing a two-phase recovery plan. Phase 2 (from 2026) aims to reset budgets to sustainable levels, repay temporary borrowing, restrict new unsupported borrowing, and rebuild reserves to a prudent target of £50 million.
findings.matters: Indicates past reserve depletion, reliance on temporary borrowing, and a multi-year timeframe required to restore the HRA to financial sustainability; material for assessing refinancing risk.
findings.figures: £50 million prudent reserve target
findings.quote: Phase 2, commencing in 2026, will focus on resetting both revenue and capital budgets to sustainable levels, repaying temporary borrowing, restricting new unsupported borrowing, and rebuilding reserves to a prudent target level of £50 million.

findings.headline: Revenue contribution to capital cut by £9.2 million, requiring asset disposal to fund capital programme
findings.detail: The council has implemented a £9.2m reduction in revenue contributions to capital to mitigate the in-year deficit. This reduction will require the council to find matching funding elsewhere, with asset disposal identified as the most likely source.
findings.matters: Signals capital investment constraints and reliance on asset sales rather than sustainable revenue funding; suggests the capital programme cannot be funded from current operations.
findings.figures: £9.2 million reduction in revenue contributions to capital
findings.quote: a £9.2 million reduction in revenue contributions to capital was implemented. This will necessitate the identification of a matching amount of funding for the capital programme to compensate, most likely through additional asset disposal.

findings.headline: Void volumes and lettings delays reducing rental income, a key driver of the deficit
findings.detail: The council reports increases in void volumes, extended turnaround times, and delays in letting new stock. These income pressures, combined with delays in billing major works accounts, are core to the period 4 deficit.
findings.matters: Rental income is the HRA's primary revenue source; delays and voids reduce cash available for debt service and capital investment without requiring savings elsewhere.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this paper
findings.quote: an increase in void volumes, extended turnaround times, and delays in letting new stock and billing major works accounts.

findings.headline: Repairs and maintenance overspend of £6.6 million due to ageing stock and regulatory compliance
findings.detail: The expenditure side of the deficit is driven largely by repairs costs rising faster than budgeted. The council attributes this to the age of the housing stock and rising costs tied to regulatory compliance requirements.
findings.matters: Signals ongoing capital maintenance pressures and suggests a potential backlog of condition-related investment in an already-stretched budget.
findings.figures: £6.6 million overspend on repairs and maintenance
findings.quote: there was a £6.6 million overspend on repairs and maintenance, largely due to the ageing housing stock and rising costs associated with regulatory compliance.

findings.headline: HRA 2025-26 forecast deficit of £10.1 million with only marginal improvement expected
findings.detail: Period 4 (July 2025) forecast a £10.1m deficit. The latest period 6 forecast (September) shows slight improvement, but the council acknowledges risks remain—particularly within repairs and maintenance—and further mitigations will be necessary to stay within cash limits. No specific period 6 figure given.
findings.matters: The HRA is ring-fenced and self-financing; a structural deficit of this scale threatens reserves and future borrowing capacity for housing investment.
findings.figures: £10.1 million deficit (period 4, July 2025)
findings.quote: The last reported position to Cabinet was period 4 (July 2025), which forecast a £10.1 million deficit.

findings.headline: Council plans c.£145m Housing Revenue Account borrowing in second half of year at current elevated interest rates
findings.detail: The report explicitly states that the majority of new borrowing expected in the remainder of 2025-26 will be for the Housing Revenue Account, estimated at c.£145m. No new PWLB borrowing has been taken in the first half due to higher-than-anticipated cash balances. Current PWLB HRA rates are set at gilt yields (currently 5.4% on 30-year debt) plus a 0.4% margin.
findings.matters: This represents a material borrowing decision at elevated rates, which will increase annual debt service costs and affect the council's debt servicing position going forward.
findings.figures: c.£145m estimated HRA borrowing; PWLB HRA rate: gilt rate +0.4% (currently ~5.8% for 30-year borrowing)
findings.quote: The majority of new borrowing expected in the remainder of the year will be for the Housing Revenue Account and is estimated to be c.£145m.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit of £5.8m as at March 2025; maintained schools at financial risk requiring Licensed Deficit Framework
findings.detail: The DSG cumulative deficit reached £5.8m by 31 March 2025, up from £14m received in Safety Valve grants. The council faces financial risk from maintained schools that close with deficit balances, and has established a Licensed Deficit Framework to support schools in financial difficulty as pupil numbers decline across London.
findings.matters: While £5.8m is manageable, the underlying driver (declining pupil numbers) is structural. Schools closures create contingent liability if deficits crystallise.
findings.figures: DSG cumulative deficit £5.8m; £1.8m received in 2024-25 under Safety Valve Agreement
findings.quote: the council remains at financial risk for any maintained schools that close with deficit balances

findings.headline: Internal audit opinion delivers only moderate assurance on control frameworks, not full assurance
findings.detail: The Chief Audit Executive's opinion provides moderate assurance on the adequacy and effectiveness of internal controls, risk management and governance. Moderate assurance denotes a sound system designed to meet objectives with controls applied consistently, but is not full/high assurance.
findings.matters: Moderate rather than full assurance indicates control gaps remain. Combined with prior issues (HRA overspend, TMO failures, RSH downgrade), this suggests the control environment has material weaknesses.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: The audit opinion overall, provides moderate assurance. This denotes that that there is a sound system of internal control, designed to meet the council's objectives, that controls are being applied consistently across various services.

findings.headline: Central government funding settlement expected to bring substantial reduction from 2026-27 onwards through business rates reset and spending restraint
findings.detail: The council expects substantial cuts to central government funding from April 2026 following the planned business rates reset. The current spending review limits increases to 3.1% in 2025-26, dropping to 1.3% annually thereafter. The Institute for Fiscal Studies predicted unprotected services like local government could face 3.5% annual real-terms cuts. Council notes the provisional funding settlement is not due until November/December 2025.
findings.matters: Structural funding cuts of this scale will require service reductions or Council Tax rises beyond stated assumptions. This creates downside risk to medium-term financial plans and council resilience.
findings.figures: 3.1% increase 2025-26; 1.3% per year thereafter; IFS predicted up to 3.5% annual cuts in unprotected areas
findings.quote: the council is likely to face a substantial reduction in central government funding. This reduction is expected to be introduced gradually over a three-year transitional period.

findings.headline: Tenant Management Organisations (TMOs) experienced significant governance failures causing financial and reputational harm, requiring restructured oversight
findings.detail: The council identified significant deficiencies in TMO management and governance that caused material financial and reputational harm. In response, the council created a specialist TMO Governance Team, introduced mandatory quarterly management accounts, required yearly business plans, and implemented a detailed contract monitoring checklist. This indicates prior control failures in a material service delivery arm.
findings.matters: TMO governance failures demonstrate past weakness in oversight of contracted services. The remedial measures suggest controls are now tighter, but the prior incidents indicate governance gaps that affected finances.
findings.figures: Not quantified; issues reported to Audit Committee 3 February 2025
findings.quote: significant deficiencies in the management and governance of TMOs which have caused significant financial and reputational harm to the council and impaired the ability of TMOs to continue to provide high quality landlord services

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation overspend of £9.5m continuing as demand driven by homelessness crisis shows no signs of abating
findings.detail: Southwark spent £9.5m over budget on temporary accommodation in 2023-24. This reflects a London-wide pressure: all London councils are projected to overspend by £330m (60% above budget) on homelessness costs. The document identifies the cost drivers as growing national homelessness, unaffordable private rents, and Local Housing Allowance caps that leave welfare benefits insufficient to cover rent.
findings.matters: This is a structural demand pressure, not a one-off. A £3m additional grant for 2025-26 will not close the gap. Councils with significant TA liabilities face ongoing budget pressures that cannot be contained through efficiency alone.
findings.figures: £9.5m overspend 2023-24 at Southwark; £330m London-wide overspend (60% over budget)
findings.quote: the cost and demand for temporary accommodation remains unremitting, driven by the growing national homelessness crisis, unaffordable private sector rented accommodation and restrictions on Local Housing Allowance (LHA) rates

news_drafts.lead: Ombudsman complaints are leading indicators of service failure and governance breakdown; rapid escalation suggests systemic issues that may trigger further regulatory action

news_drafts.lead: Reserve depletion is accelerating; financial sustainability now depends on successful execution of transformation programmes that have not yet been proven to deliver savings
